items.title: It was a busy morning for the Chattanooga Fire Department as firefighters fought back-to-back house fires.  The first fi...
items.content_text:
It was a busy morning for the Chattanooga Fire Department as firefighters fought back-to-back house fires. 
 The first fire was reported at 8:47 AM on 10/13/26 at a duplex in the 1800 block of Citico Avenue in the East Chattanooga area. First arriving units found smoke and fire coming from the back of the structure. Firefighters initiated an interior attack and took another line to the rear of the residence where flames were through the collapsed roof. Searches were conducted and no one was found inside on either side of the duplex. Fire officials learned that both sides were vacant. By 9:10 AM, the fire was out. 
 Engine 4, Engine 5, Engine 10, Squad 1, Ladder 1, Battalion 1, Battalion 3, CFD Investigations, CFD Training Division, and CFD Supply responded, along with CPD, HCEMS, and EPB. There were no injuries. 
 As crews were wrapping up operations on Citico Avenue, another house fire was reported at 9:29 AM in the 1500 block of South Highland Park Avenue off Main Street. Callers to 911 indicated that flames were visible through the front doors and windows of the home. A plume of smoke could be seen by responding companies. On the scene, crews found fire in the front of the structure. Officials quickly learned that one person was home at the time of the fire, but they made it out safely. Primary attack was made through the front door and crews continued working to extinguish the blaze. Their efforts were made difficult by the amount of contents inside the residence. By 10:01 AM, the fire was out. One adult was displaced and will be receiving assistance from the American Red Cross. The cause of the fire is under investigation. 
 Engine 1, Squad 13, Engine 9, Engine 14, Squad 1, Engine 5, Squad 20, Engine 3, Battalion 1, Battalion 2, CFD Investigations, CFD Training Division, and CFD Supply responded, along with CPD, HCEMS, and EBP. There were no injuries. 
 Fire investigators do not believe the two fires are connected in any way. Thanks to Red Shift companies for their hard work and adaptability in moving from one response to another.

Trade increasingly runs on data. 
 For goods to flow, trusted information needs to flow about how a product was made, where key inputs originated and what regulations it complies with. 
 And the demand for information is growing.
 Over the last decade, environment-related technical requirements have increased by more than 60%.
 Our new #OECD report, Better Borders for Trade, Traceability and Enforcement, shows that border systems are not keeping pace.
 Policymakers already have trade facilitation tools at their disposal to speed things up and lower costs for businesses and government:
 ➡️ Integrating new information requirements into existing streamlined systems
 ➡️ Using risk-based approaches
 ➡️ Expanding international regulatory co-operation
 Read the report to find out more: https://brnw.ch/21x6n6H

items.content_text:
Regional collaboration doesn't stop at state lines.

Last week, our SETD team joined leaders from Northwest Georgia, Southeast Tennessee and Northeast Alabama for Thrive Regional Partnership's 2026 Tri-State Summit.

Throughout the Summit, our team had opportunities to contribute to conversations and experiences highlighting the importance of working together across communities.

A few highlights included:
- A regional gathering of mayors from across the tri-state to discuss shared challenges and opportunities.
- Our Deputy Director Kelly Puckett moderating a panel on civic experiments and how locally driven ideas are bringing communities together.
- Our tourism coordinator participating in a paddle excursion down the Hiwassee River, sharing some insight into the Southeast Tennessee Tourism Association (SETTA), and listening to a panel explore the role tourism plays in our region's communities and economies.

These moments reflect the many ways regional collaboration takes shape, through local leadership, creative community initiatives, and the experiences that make our region unique.

We are happy to continue building a collaborative partnership with Thrive Regional Partnership and thank you for bringing together leaders and partners committed to strengthening the communities we call home.

We know it's spooky season, but driving shouldn't be a nightmare! The number of people driving without their lights on during recent foggy conditions has been scary. 
 Keep these safety tips in mind when driving in fog.
 1. Turn your headlights on. This not only helps you see but also allows others to see you because your taillights are on.
 2. Leave plenty of room between you and the car in front of you in case there are sudden stops.
 3. Slow down and give yourself some extra time to get where you're going. 
 Simple steps like these can help everyone reach their final destination safely.

items.title: On Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we’re highlighting a powerful story found within one of Chattanooga’s most meaningful public...
items.content_text:
On Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we’re highlighting a powerful story found within one of Chattanooga’s most meaningful public artworks.
 At the bottom of The Passage at Ross’s Landing, a steel water spider rests beneath the shallow pool. Designed by Cherokee artist Demos Glass, the sculpture draws inspiration from ancient shell carvings discovered at the Dallas archaeological site right here in Hamilton County.
 In Cherokee storytelling, the Water Spider helped bring fire to the world when other animals could not. Using a small bowl she wove and carried on her back, she crossed the water, collected an ember, and returned with the gift of fire.
 Her story is one of courage, ingenuity, and perseverance.
 Created in 2005 by Team Gadugi, a group of Cherokee artists, The Passage honors Indigenous history, culture, and the Cherokee people whose forced removal is part of Chattanooga’s history.
 Today, we honor the Indigenous peoples who have called this region home for generations and the Native communities whose cultures, stories, and artistic traditions continue to thrive.
 The next time you visit The Passage, take a closer look. There are stories beneath the surface.
 #IndigenousPeoplesDay #PublicArtChattanooga #ThePassage #Chattanooga

items.title: Red Bank Mourns the Passing of Longtime City Judge Johnny D. Houston, Jr. RED BANK, TN – The City of Red Bank mourns the...
items.content_text:
Red Bank Mourns the Passing of Longtime City Judge Johnny D. Houston, Jr.
 RED BANK, TN – The City of Red Bank mourns the passing of longtime City Judge Johnny D. Houston, Jr., who died Sunday, October 11, 2026.
 Judge Houston was first appointed to serve as Red Bank City Judge in 2000 and subsequently was elected to three consecutive eight-year terms, most recently winning reelection in August 2022.
 For more than 25 years, Judge Houston was a familiar and respected presence in Red Bank. His roots in the community preceded his judicial service. He previously served as president of the Red Bank Chamber of Commerce and coached youth sports in Red Bank and North Chattanooga.
 His connection to Red Bank was also evident in the everyday places where people knew him. In recent years, he could frequently be found enjoying Red Bank’s pickleball courts. His law practice was distinctly Red Bank as well, located in a beautiful historic home along Dayton Boulevard. Those connections made him more than the City Judge. He was very much a part of the everyday life of the community he served.
 “Johnny Houston gave an extraordinary portion of his life to Red Bank,” said City Manager Martin Granum. “For more than two decades, generations of Red Bank residents knew him as Judge Houston, but they also knew him as a neighbor, attorney, coach, and familiar face around town. His passing marks the end of a remarkable period of service to our city, and we will remember him with gratitude and love. Our thoughts are especially with his family, friends, and colleagues during this difficult time.”
 Judge Houston graduated from the University of Tennessee at Knoxville in 1986 and Memphis State University Law School in 1989. He had been a Chattanooga-area resident since 1989 and maintained his law practice in Red Bank.
 "My sincerest condolences to Casey and Judge Houston's family,” said Red Bank City Judge Bryan Hoss.  “For years, Judge Houston was a pillar in our legal community here in Hamilton County.  He loved representing Red Bank as their Judge and was not only well respected, but many of us considered him a dear friend and colleague.  For me personally, it was an honor when Red Bank asked me to step into his shoes as the next Judge.  Rest in peace, Johnny."
 The City of Red Bank extends its deepest sympathies to Judge Houston’s family and joins the broader community and legal community in mourning his passing, celebrating his life and recognizing his many years of dedicated service to Red Bank.

items.title: HONORING OUR FALLEN: Senior Firefighter Chad Crisp was added to the Tennessee Fallen Firefighter Memorial in Bell Buckle...
items.content_text:
HONORING OUR FALLEN: Senior Firefighter Chad Crisp was added to the Tennessee Fallen Firefighter Memorial in Bell Buckle, TN this past weekend. We lost Chad in 2020 after a brave battle with occupational cancer. 
 For the Crisp family, it was incredibly special to see Chad remembered in this way. His wife, Leah, wrote this:
 “While we honor Chad and his lifelong dedication to service, we also want to recognize the advocates who worked tirelessly to change policy so Chad could be included.
 Changes to presumptive illness laws at both the state and federal levels have started closing the gap in coverage for so many fire families facing a cancer diagnosis.
 Perhaps the most significant change is happening right here at home. The City of Chattanooga now includes comprehensive cancer coverage in its worker's compensation policy for firefighters—covering all types of cancer. To my knowledge, this level of coverage is limited to only a couple of municipalities statewide. Additionally, the Chattanooga Fire Department has implemented new safety procedures and early detection screenings to protect our firefighters.
 Chattanooga put words into action, providing meaningful support for firefighters and their families when it matters most.
 As we remember Chad, we also celebrate the dedication of those who continue to honor his memory by creating a safer path for those who follow in his footsteps.”

items.content_text:
Today we welcomed representatives from nine global cities for the first day of the 11th #Urban95Academy residence week.
The cohort is made up of a diverse group of municipal leaders each committed to improving the lives of children and those who care for them. 
In Aqaba, Jordan the team is working to bridge the gap between a growing young population but a perceived “lack of public space” and “poor pedestrian environment” according to the city’s master plan. 
In Baguio City, Philippines the team want to increase the number of children and families accessing early childhood services by transforming existing infrastructure in a pilot location to bring services together and link them to welcoming public spaces. 
In Cairo, Egypt the team’s challenge is to address what they describe as a critical urban-child development crisis. Rapid urbanisation in the city has contributed to traffic congestion, air pollution and a near absence of safe mobility for families, the negative impacts are particularly felt by children with disabilities. 
In Helsinki, Finland the team is looking at how to strengthen participatory placemaking, with further involvement of children and specifically at how urban lighting can enhance the wellbeing of children. 
In Jarinu, Brazil the team wants to improve access to public services to young children and families. Rapid population growth in the city has extended the distance between residential areas and essential early childhood services, the team’s aim is to reorganise services around territories where children are. 
In Kuching South, Malaysia the team is working to address challenges around a lack of parental and caregiver interaction with young children, insufficient walkability and limited opportunities for outdoor play among other.
In Lo Espejo, Chile the team aims to create an early childhood plaza to give residents access to much needed safe outdoor space. The plaza will offer children and families nature-rich space in the city where they can access programming to connect them to public spaces. 
In Rio de Janeiro, Brazil the team is working to reverse the perceived lack of safety in the city that is a result of high-quality public spaces and a shortage of play spaces. 
A team representing Transport for London  is addressing London’s falling child population from a transport perspective centering the function of transport to connect families to childcare, healthcare, public space and essential services. The team is contributing to the TFL’s Streets for Children Toolkit to ensure that transport is recognised as crucial infrastructure for healthy childhoods and family wellbeing.

items.content_text:
Thank you, Chattanooga NAACP, for honoring School Resource Deputy Marty Ray at the 37th Annual Ruby Hurley Image Awards for his outstanding service to Hamilton County over the weekend.
 Deputy Ray exemplifies the qualities representative of the Ralph Cothran Civil Service Officer of the Year.
 “Deputy Ray has proudly served at Brainerd High School for seventeen years. During that time, he has done far more than maintain safety on campus. He has mentored students, built relationships with families and school staff, and become a trusted presence in the lives of countless young people. As Deputy Ray plans to retire later this year, there is no greater time to recognize his dedication and service to Hamilton County, and his absence will leave a challenging void to fill at both Brainerd High School and within the School Resource Deputy unit,” stated Captain Jamie Fields.

items.content_text:
Only 40% of people across OECD countries trust their national government. At the same time, governments are being asked to navigate rapid technological change, AI, demographic shifts, environmental challenges and geopolitical uncertainty. 
 Governments are responding to these pressures, but many are finding it difficult to keep pace with today’s challenges. A deep transformation of how governments work is underway, building on the opportunities created by AI and a new generation of public servants with fresh talent.  
 Our new report, #GovernmentUnstuck: The Next Frontier of Government Transformation, explores the cutting-edge practices that are helping to shape a coherent way forward for public administration that is more connected to citizens, simpler to navigate, more flexible in how it uses resources, and better prepared for the future.  
 Drawing on evidence from over 40 countries, the report identifies practical examples of how governments are making progress across four critical areas: 
 ➡️ Trusted and connected digital technologies and data  
 ➡️ Agile government operating systems 
 ➡️ Skilled and empowered public servants  
 ➡️ Meaningful and strategic citizen engagement 
 Read the report in full: https://brnw.ch/21x6kYV

The world is changing faster than government systems were designed to.
 Governments today face growing complexity, rising expectations and constant change. Yet many of the systems and structures they rely on were designed for a different era.  
 The upcoming report Government Unstuck: The Next Frontier of Government Transformation explores how public administrations can become more connected to citizens, simpler to navigate, more flexible in how they use resources, and better prepared for the future.  
 Drawing on case studies from across #OECD countries, the report highlights the cutting-edge practices that are helping governments strengthen trust, anticipate change and adapt in a rapidly evolving world.  
 Meeting rising expectations will require governments to rethink how they operate, not just expand what they do.
 📅 12 October 2026, 9:15 CEST| OECD Conference Centre, Paris  
 Register for the launch event at the opening session of the 2026 OECD Global Forum on Building Trust and Reinforcing Democracy on #GovernmentUnstuck: https://brnw.ch/21x6jI8

Young people’s mental health has been deteriorating for over a decade.
 Between 2012 and 2022, youth mental health indicators worsened by an average of 3% to 16% annually across nine OECD countries with comparable data.
 What is driving this trend? New #OECD research points to a combination of factors, including socio-economic pressures, bullying, academic stress and the growing influence of digital environments.
 There is no single solution. But stronger prevention, supportive schools and families, and earlier access to youth-friendly mental health services can make a difference.
 On #WorldMentalHealthDay, explore how OECD research can help countries better protect and support young people’s #MentalHealth.
 Learn more: https://brnw.ch/21x6jdq

HCSO SRD Involved in Pursuit Starting at Brainerd High School, Juvenile Suspect Arrested
 Hamilton County, TN – Earlier today, at approximately 3:15 p.m., the HCSO School Resource Deputy assigned to Brainerd High School observed a juvenile female driving recklessly through the school’s parking lot in an apparent attempt to strike an individual with her vehicle. Preliminary evidence indicates that the suspect had targeted this individual that they were attempting to run over.
 The driver failed to stop when the SRD activated their vehicle’s emergency lights and siren, initiating a pursuit. The suspect's vehicle was finally brought to a stop on Shepherd Road, where they were taken into custody.
 The juvenile suspect was arrested and charged with the following:
 -  Aggravated Domestic Assault

Halloween Trail Fest Canceled Saturday; Enterprise South Opening Delayed Sunday
 HAMILTON COUNTY, Tenn. — Hamilton County Parks & Recreation is coordinating with the Office of Emergency Management, the National Weather Service and local meteorologists to prepare for potential impacts from Hurricane Isaias.
 Halloween Trail Fest is canceled Saturday, October 10. Enterprise South Nature Park will open on a two-hour delay Sunday, October 11, allowing staff to assess conditions and address potential hazards, including fallen trees, debris and blocked trails. While conditions may improve throughout the day, the department is taking a cautious approach with public safety as its top priority. Additional closures may be necessary based on conditions.
 “Halloween Trail Fest is a cherished fall break tradition, and our Enterprise South team has invested tremendous time and creativity into this experience,” said Allison Harr, Superintendent of Enterprise South Nature Park. “We share our community’s disappointment; however public safety is our top priority.”
 Visitors are asked to respect the delayed opening and check the Hamilton County Parks & Recreation’s official channels for updates including the Enterprise South Nature Park official Page.
